title: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
desc: Separates citation accuracy, argument quality and empirical error rates, with sanctions varying by authority, candour and correction.

kps.k: The central proposition is that AI can assist legal work, but it cannot assume responsibility for its accuracy.
kps.d: Noland, Wadsworth, Fletcher and professional guidance distinguish permissible research or drafting assistance from reliance on unchecked output. They apply existing duties of reasonable inquiry, competence and candour rather than treating AI use itself as misconduct. Verification requires reading underlying authorities, checking their current status and confirming that they support the asserted proposition—not merely finding a plausible citation. Cassata expressly makes accountability independent of whether AI authorship can be proved.

qs.q: Although we take counsel at his word—and although there is  nothing inherently wrong with an attorney appropriately using  AI in a law practice—before filing any court document, an  attorney must “carefully check every case citation, fact, and  argument to make sure that they are correct and proper.
qs.a: Noland v. Land of the Free, L.P., 114 Cal. App. 5th 426, 336 Cal. Rptr. 3d 897 (2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: As attorneys transition to the world of AI, the duty to check their sources  and make a reasonable inquiry into existing law remains unchanged.
qs.a: Wadsworth v. Walmart — sanctions where the hallucinated citations came from a law firm's internal AI platform · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The debate extends beyond invented cases to misleading uses of genuine authorities, and citation accuracy remains distinct from argument quality.
kps.d: Hallucination-Free? challenges vendor claims that authentic links establish reliable answers: retrieved sources can contradict the generated conclusion, and models can confuse rejected arguments with holdings or overlook controlling authority. Lnu expressly adopts the study’s broader terminology encompassing substantive inaccuracies; that usage should not obscure the distinction between fabrication and faulty legal analysis. Conversely, A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law argues that false citations need not make surrounding arguments incorrect. Whiting preserves a related legal distinction: fabricated citations remain sanctionable even where legitimate authorities might support the appeal. Thinking Like a Lawyer adds that eliminating fabricated sources does not establish high-quality legal work.

qs.q: LexisNexis claims that its AI tool provides “linked hallucination-free legal citations” (LexisNexis, 2023), but, as we demonstrate below, this claim can only be true in the most narrow sense of “hallucination,” in that their tool does indeed link to real legal documents.9 If those linked sources are irrelevant, or even contradict the AI tool’s claims, the tool has, in our sense, engaged in a hallucination.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

qs.q: We thus adopt the broader definition of hallucinations proposed by Magesh et al.
qs.a: Lnu v. Blanche, No. 24-4790 (9th Cir. June 3, 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Empirical research supports persistent, task-dependent errors, not a single legal-AI error rate or an assured improvement trajectory.
kps.d: Hallucination-Free? finds that retrieval augmentation improves performance but leaves substantial errors in the three commercial products tested; low error frequency can also reflect frequent refusals. Who Checks the Citations? tests eight ChatGPT generations from late 2023 through late 2025 on 92 drafting prompts and reports citation-fabrication rates of 1.23% for a mid-2024 GPT-4o release and 6.57% for GPT-5.1. Its prompts reconstruct problematic filings, and its generation measure excludes subtler unsupported propositions. These results differ in task, denominator and error definition from legal-research evaluations. Sources disagree about the outlook: some characterise fabrication as structural, while Thinking Like a Lawyer reports substantial source-reliability gains from RAG. Neither position establishes that future systems will eliminate errors or remain at historical rates.

qs.q: Our findings, summarized in Figure 1, reveal a more nuanced reality than the one presented by these providers: while RAG appears to improve the performance of language models in answering legal queries, the hallucination problem persists at significant levels.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Through a controlled experiment querying eight generations of ChatGPT models on 92 legal drafting prompts, we find that hallucination rates are no longer consistently decreasing across model generations, with GPT-5.1 producing hallucinated citations at a significantly higher rate than the best mid-2024 GPT-4o release (p = 0.001).
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Court incidents establish concrete consequences, but neither incident counts nor repeated reporting measure overall AI reliability.
kps.d: Charlotin’s database records judicial treatment of false AI-related material, including some decisions where AI use remains alleged or inferred. Its supplied 2026 snapshot identifies 1,174 cases but expressly excludes the wider universe of false citations and AI-assisted filings. Other sources report different dates, populations and totals from the same evolving resource; these counts should not be added together. The records document struck briefs, adverse costs, disciplinary referrals and dismissals. Courts also identify diverted judicial resources, opposing-party expenses and reputational risks. The Verification-Value Paradox treats the database as an indicator of reprimand trends while questioning its methodological transparency, not as a comprehensive prevalence estimate.

qs.q: While seeking to be exhaustive (**1174** cases identified so far), it is a work in progress and will expand as new examples emerge.

kps.k: Sanctions depend on the applicable authority and circumstances; candour and correction matter alongside the initial error.
kps.d: Noland rejects ignorance and lack of deceptive intent as sufficient answers to a verification failure, while Fletcher orders a $2,500 sanction. Yet Al-Hamim declines sanctions and gives a prospective warning, and the surveyed Cohen decision declines sanctions because it finds no bad faith despite negligence. Accounts of Mata, Crabill and Lacey emphasise continued reliance, incomplete correction or misleading explanations after problems surfaced. These differences do not establish a universal culpability threshold. Show-cause orders and disciplinary referrals likewise remain distinct from completed sanctions or final disciplinary findings. Oregon’s ethics opinion requires notification and correction of discovered false statements, subject to client confidentiality.

kps.k: Responsibility extends through supervision and supplied material, making operational review more important than an AI policy alone.
kps.d: Johnson’s supplied headnotes describe sanctions against lawyers who did not know a colleague had used AI but failed to check filings bearing their names. The malpractice commentary reports similar exposure for supervisors and local counsel, including firms with restrictive AI policies. Kohls suggests that reasonable inquiry may require asking witnesses about AI-assisted declarations and their checking practices, rather than announcing a categorical requirement. The Promise and the Peril proposes additional explanations for failures: presentation-only review, trust in colleagues, workload and growing confidence in fluent output can displace intended checking. Its Dayal example shows that obtaining a verification report does not ensure anyone uses it. These are case illustrations and proposed mechanisms, not quantified causal effects.

qs.q: Lawyers have been sanctioned despite being in firms with strict AI usage policies, 37 and local counsel have been sanctioned for failure to review and catch the AI hallucinations in the filings of the primary counsel on the case.
qs.a: AI and Legal Malpractice: Are We Due for a Reckoning? · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The principal regulatory disagreement concerns AI-specific disclosure and restrictions, not whether submissions must be accurate.
kps.d: Reported standing orders require disclosure, accuracy certification or records identifying AI-drafted passages. The supplied order labelled Starr actually attributes its substantive requirements to Judge Peter Kang. By contrast, the October 2025 judicial-office-holder guidance makes disclosure context-dependent. A Fifth Circuit rulemaking commenter favours technology-neutral checking, arguing that false citations predate AI, proprietary tools obscure AI use, and disclosure could burden work product or deter useful research. Browning accepts the duplication objection but highlights judges’ concerns about unrepresented litigants; Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence criticises aggressive restrictions. The supplied Fifth Circuit passages establish a proposal and objections, not the court’s eventual decision or reasoning.

kps.k: Automated checking can support human verification, but its limitations shift attention to legal-data access and transparent testing.
kps.d: Who Checks the Citations? introduces 1,300 brief excerpts with injected errors and tests downstream checking systems. Its abstract reports GPT-5 agentic recall of 84.4%, F1 of 55.0% and an average of 15.3 steps per excerpt; a separate conclusion reports best-model F1 of 68.8%, which should not be conflated with that GPT-5 result. Substantive misrepresentation and pinpoint checking remain difficult. Database coverage also creates false positives: absence from CourtListener does not establish fabrication. The authors propose draft screening, accessible tools and broader public legal data. Hallucination-Free? separately calls for public evaluations and precise vendor claims. These proposals support, rather than replace, lawyers’ final review.

qs.q: • We introduce a dataset of 1,300 legal brief excerpts with injected hallucinations to support eval-       uation and auditing of citation verification systems, grounded in a taxonomy of legal citation       hallucinations derived from real court filings.

kps.k: Equal verification duties create an access-to-justice tension when litigants lack the expertise or resources to fulfil them.
kps.d: Al-Hamim and other reported rulings retain procedural responsibility for self-represented filers. Artificial Access to Justice argues that a layperson may be unable to judge whether even genuine authorities support a claim, making certification a formal act without substantive comprehension. It reports dismissal of 61.1% of AI-flagged complaints versus 53.6% of unflagged complaints in its post-AI comparison, but the supplied material does not establish causation. Who Checks the Citations? argues that sanctions alone cannot remedy unequal checking capacity and recommends education, free case law and accessible tools. Generative AI and the Future of the Courts instead stresses prospective benefits from forms, research and plain-language explanations. The disagreement concerns whether cheaper participation delivers meaningful assistance, not whether unmet civil legal need exists.

kps.k: Faster production can increase institutional checking burdens even as individual outputs improve, while accuracy safeguards leave other risks unresolved.
kps.d: Who Checks the Citations? observes more numerous and less familiar citations in newer-model drafts and predicts that cheaper drafting could increase total filing volume. Unperformed checks then fall to opponents, clerks and judges. Courts-focused commentary recommends planning for additional legally trained staff and distinguishes citation scrutiny from authentication of deepfake evidence. Judicial guidance also warns about concealed prompts and personal responsibility for outputs. Separately, confidentiality and privilege require their own safeguards; accurate text does not make disclosure of client information safe. Malpractice and vendor-liability commentary projects further financial exposure, but incident inventories do not establish paid insurance losses or general provider liability.

qs.q: Newer models generate more citations per document than their predecessors, drawn from a broader and less canonical set of cases that are individually harder to verify (Figure 2).
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

qs.q: To deal with the influx, courts should anticipate the need for an increase in legally-trained court staff to assist judges in evaluating legal citations for their relevance and weight.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Future of the Courts: Responsibilities and Possibilities · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an:
The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the synthesis’s principal proposition that AI may assist legal work but cannot assume responsibility for accuracy. They commonly ground that position in evidence that fabricated authorities persist, that authentic citations may still be irrelevant, contradictory or mischaracterised, and that fluent presentation is not equivalent to sound legal reasoning. They also consistently separate task-specific benchmark results from court incidents: experimental error rates depend on models, prompts, tasks and definitions, while sanctions databases document consequences rather than overall prevalence.

This voice materially builds on the proposition in several ways. Empirical studies test commercial legal-research products, multiple model generations and downstream agentic checking; doctrinal and litigation research explains how responsibility extends through supervision, candour and correction; and access-to-justice scholarship shows that equal verification duties can become practically unfulfillable for self-represented litigants lacking legal expertise or database access. Other work proposes mechanisms for failed checking, including cognitive offloading, trust in colleagues, workload and “verification drift,” and recommends transparent benchmarking, broader public legal-data access and accessible checking tools.

Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than the basic accuracy duty. Some sources portray hallucination as structurally inherent, while others report substantial gains from RAG or warn against basing durable institutions on current error rates. Some favour technology-neutral application of existing filing rules and criticise aggressive AI-specific restrictions; others support disclosure, certification or stronger safeguards. Access-to-justice sources range from qualified optimism about AI as a research starting point to concern that cheaper production expands formal participation without substantive gains. One scholarship-focused source redirects the inquiry toward whether even flawless AI-generated writing can evidence authorial understanding, and bibliographic-only excerpts leave some positions unclear. These differences should not be read as estimates of prevalence within academia or research.

qs.q: LexisNexis claims that its AI tool provides “linked hallucination-free legal citations” (LexisNexis, 2023), but, as we demonstrate below, this claim can only be true in the most narrow sense of “hallucination,” in that their tool does indeed link to real legal documents.9 If those linked sources are irrelevant, or even contradict the AI tool’s claims, the tool has, in our sense, engaged in a hallucination.
qs.a: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources accepts the cluster’s principal proposition: AI may assist legal drafting or research, but responsibility remains with the filer, who must verify both that authorities exist and that they support the propositions asserted. The sources commonly ground that view in reported court incidents, sanctions, disciplinary referrals and failures of supervision, while carefully distinguishing documented incidents from measured model error rates. They materially extend the proposition by tracing downstream operational and financial effects, particularly potential malpractice-insurance exposure and regulatory responses. Internal variation concerns emphasis rather than direction: some focus on rising incident reports and instruction–intent gaps; court-reporting sources distinguish fabrication from misleading use of genuine authorities and ordinary drafting errors; one press account stresses uneven sanctions and continued AI use with checking; and the insurance analysis projects a claims pipeline concentrated among small practices, while acknowledging that this is an inference rather than evidence of paid losses. These sources should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press outlets.

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-body sources accept the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develop it into operational and institutional duties. Their common reasoning is technology-neutral: AI may assist legal work, but the lawyer, filer or judicial office holder retains responsibility under existing duties of reasonable inquiry, competence and candour. Verification means examining the underlying authority and its current status and confirming that it supports the proposition asserted; a genuine citation may still be misleading if its holding or legal significance is misstated. These sources also extend responsibility through supervision, colleague-supplied material and, prospectively, AI-assisted witness declarations. Material internal variation concerns response rather than baseline accuracy: some favour AI-specific disclosure, certification and recordkeeping, while others prefer context-dependent disclosure or verification rules covering all research regardless of origin. Sanctions likewise vary with governing authority, culpability, candour and correction, from prospective warnings or no sanction to monetary penalties, disciplinary referrals and inherent-power sanctions. Several sources additionally develop broader implications—correction duties, court workload, unrepresented litigants’ limited verification capacity, deepfake authentication, fairness and judicial transparency—while a few fragmentary or expressly noncommittal sources provide only evidence consistent with the proposition. These materials are a curated set and should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the principal proposition that AI may assist legal work but cannot assume responsibility for accuracy. It treats independent human verification—particularly checking generated content against primary legal authorities—as mandatory before reliance, and locates accountability in existing duties such as filing certification and technological competence rather than viewing AI use itself as misconduct. It also extends the caution beyond lawyers to judges and self-represented litigants. Within the source, the main variation is an additional vendor-oriented claim that legal-specific platforms provide stronger safeguards than consumer tools. That claim may qualify the level of risk associated with platform choice, but it does not displace the need for human review; moreover, the supplied passage provides no comparative measurements to substantiate the claimed reliability advantage. Because this is one curated legal-tech vendor source, its position should not be treated as representative of vendors generally.

qs.q: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and its state counterparts establish clear certification requirements for court filings, making attorneys personally responsible for verifying all submitted content, regardless of its technological origin.
qs.a: From 'trust but verify' to 'do not trust until verified': How the legal profession is redefining AI accountability · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources broadly support the proposition that generative AI may assist legal work but cannot bear responsibility for the accuracy of legal submissions. Courts and professional guidance repeatedly place verification, reasonable inquiry and candour on lawyers and, often, self-represented filers. Their common rationale is that fluent, conventionally formatted output can conceal nonexistent authorities, distorted holdings, unsupported assertions or omitted contrary precedent; checking therefore must reach the underlying authority and its actual relevance, not merely confirm that a citation looks plausible or exists. Court incidents establish concrete consequences but are illustrations rather than measurements of overall AI reliability, and the period’s research-oriented sources call for systematic, task-sensitive evaluation rather than inferring a single error rate from sanctions cases.

Material internal variation concerns consequences and governance rather than the basic accuracy duty. Sanctions range from substantial penalties to prospective warnings or no sanction where bad faith is absent, with post-discovery correction and candour affecting outcomes. Some sources materially extend the proposition: one separates fabricated citations from the possible defensibility of the surrounding argument; others show that genuine authorities can still mislead when contrary precedent is overlooked or relevance is misunderstood. Regulatory approaches also diverge: some judicial orders require AI-specific disclosure, recordkeeping and certification, while critics prefer technology-neutral human verification under existing rules and warn that AI-specific restrictions may burden work product or deter beneficial use. Access-to-justice commentary exposes a further tension between holding self-represented litigants to ordinary standards and their limited capacity to evaluate authorities, while differing over whether AI will reduce or deepen that disadvantage. These variations do not amount to opposition to the principal proposition.

qs.q: Attorneys may  instead use generative AI as a starting point and must independently review case citations,  arguments and any other information/output produced by generative AI.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: “Citing nonexistent case law or misrepresenting the holdings of a case is making a false statement to a court[;] [i]t does not matter if [generative A.I.] told you so.” Maura R.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that AI may assist legal work but cannot assume responsibility for accuracy, and they materially develop it in several directions. Courts and professional guidance apply existing duties of competence, reasonable inquiry and candour to require substantive verification: users must confirm not only that authorities exist, but that they remain good law and support the propositions asserted. Empirical and analytical sources reinforce the distinction between authentic citations and reliable legal analysis, showing that retrieval-augmented systems can reduce fabrication while still retrieving irrelevant or contradictory sources or misinterpreting genuine authority. The period’s case law further extends responsibility through supervision, filings bearing a lawyer’s name and AI-assisted witness declarations, while research on “verification drift” identifies plausible tone, trust in colleagues, workload and cognitive offloading as mechanisms by which checking can fail. Material variation concerns implementation and outlook rather than the core duty: some sources characterise fabrication as inherent, whereas others report substantial improvements from RAG; some favour disclosure or certification requirements, while judicial guidance makes disclosure context-dependent; and sanctions vary with governing authority, culpability, candour and corrective action. Access-to-justice sources expose a further tension between formally equal verification duties and the limited expertise or research access of self-represented litigants. One bibliographic project hub provides too little attributable argument to classify, but it does not counter the broader 2025 development of the proposition.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI may assist legal work but cannot bear responsibility for accuracy, and materially develop it. Court decisions and incident records connect failures to verify fabricated citations, false quotations and unsupported uses of genuine authorities with sanctions, struck filings, dismissal, costs and disciplinary referrals. They reinforce a technology-neutral account: responsibility follows the signer and can extend through supervision or local-counsel review even where personal AI use is absent or unproved. Empirical work adds task-specific evidence that citation errors do not decline consistently across model generations and that automated, including agentic, checking improves detection but remains imperfect, resource-intensive and especially weak on subtle substantive errors. Other sources extend the analysis to unequal verification capacity among self-represented litigants, broader court workloads, privilege and malpractice-insurance risks. Material variation concerns remedies and framing rather than the basic accuracy duty: some sources favour existing professional rules while others discuss AI-specific certification or structural support; some anticipate continuing technical limits while another expects rapid reliability gains; and sanctions vary with legal authority, certainty of AI attribution, candour and correction. One scholarship source redirects attention to whether flawless AI-generated writing can evidence authorial understanding, and bibliography-only material remains unclear. These records are a curated selection and do not establish how prevalent any position is.
